comment: I comment to support the proposal for stricter National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for major source Primary Copper Smelters. Anytime human health is of concern, environmental justice becomes a very significant issue that must not be ignored. The EPA demographic analysis, as presented in this report, very clearly demonstrated that these Primary Copper Smelters disproportionately affect and pose cancer risks to low-income residents, Native Americans, Hispanics, and other historically marginalized groups in areas near these major sources. Toxic air emissions from these sources posed unacceptable risks when considering that pollutants may enter waters near fisheries and downstream farms that grow crops for human consumption. I also support the proposal’s guidelines to remove “SSM” exemptions for periods when factories are turned-on, shut down, and for periods of malfunction. I believe it should be clear to anyone with a level head that emissions standards should apply at all times, and that these periods of exemption have been dangerous to the health of humans and our environment.

comment:
I am submitting my comment for Docket No. EPA-HQ-OAR-2020-0430.

I am in agreement with the EPA in partitioning PM pollutants from gaseous pollutants as the gaseous contaminants cannot be detected by PM monitoring methods. The technology for gaseous monitoring instruments has made progress in leaps and bounds in detection sensitivity for parts per billion, and parts per trillion in atmospheric monitoring. Progress has also been made to implement in-line sensors on the stacks or in the pipes to monitor the contaminants during the refining process. There is no excuse to not upgrade the monitoring equipment. Scrubbers are also not that expensive relative to the profit margin to upgrade in the factory. Companies can extract all the minerals they want as long they do not harm my water, my air, my soil. Companies do not have the right to poison people.

comment:
Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OAR-2020-0430

Environmental Protection Agency

It is my understanding that the EPA is proposing to amend the 2002 National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP) for Primary Copper Smelting major sources, as well as the 2007 NESHAP for Primary Copper Smelting area sources. The EPA is requesting new emissions standards, the removal of the exemption of standards for startup, shutdown and malfunction (SSM), and that electronic reporting of performance test results be required.

The Clean Air Act (CAA) requires the EPA to regulate, review and revise the air toxics standards. The CAA and EPA have determined that risks due to Hazardous Air Pollutants from the major source category are unacceptable due to lead concentrations exceeding current standards, as well as risks due to arsenic.

I support the EPA’s request for stricter emission standards for both Primary Copper Smelting major sources and Primary Copper Smelting area sources. It is evident that the hazardous air pollutants emitted are associated with elevated cancer risks and that these risks affect nearby low-income residents, as well as Native Americans and Hispanics. I also support the EPA’s request to ensure that these standards are required at all times, by ending the exemption for SSM. I am also in favor of requiring electronic reporting of performance test results. I believe that any burden on the industry to adhere to stricter, more consistent standards would not outweigh the benefit to protecting human health and our environment. The changes that the EPA has requested are reasonable.

comment:
I support the proposal for stricter National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for major source Primary Copper Smelters.

It’s evident by the demographic analysis that the air pollutants by these major source Primary Copper Smelters are disproportionally affecting low-income and historically marginalized groups that are often forced to live in contamination-prone areas near industrial facilities such as these smelters. When it comes to environmental justice, it is crucial that these sources of toxic air waste be held to stricter regulation to better preserve the health of these communities. Furthermore, I support the progress towards holding human health in higher regard by the removal of the SSM exceptions for factories’ startup, shutdown, and malfunction periods as it would be most ideal for the minimizing of health risks to hold up the NESHAPs at all times. I am satisfied by the EPA’s support for environmental justice on this proposed rule and think it adequately addresses the pollutant issue at hand.
